repositories.title: A retry is another execution
repositories.teaching: A workflow connects actions, but a green run only says the actions returned successfully. If a network reply is lost after an upload completed, retrying can duplicate it. Give the operation a stable identifier, check its recorded result before repeating a side effect, set a timeout and cap attempts. Keep the original failure and each retry in the timeline.
repositories.question: An upload times out. Is it safe to repeat immediately?
repositories.answer: First determine whether the destination accepted it. Reuse an idempotency key or unique object identity and verify content. A timeout describes the client's observation, not whether the server completed the action.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Model source and destination backups with two local files. Run the copy twice using one backup identifier; compare checksums. Introduce a missing source and record a bounded failure.
repositories.extendedExercise: Build a disposable backup-validation workflow with an explicit timeout, bounded retries and a failure notification to a local test receiver. Trigger the same input twice and prove it cannot overwrite a good backup or create duplicate side effects. Produce a workflow diagram and failure timeline.
repositories.expectedEvidence: Prediction, observation, recovery check and explanation saved with lesson evidence.
repositories.doNotCopy: Do not copy the quick start into production: it uses mutable image tags, sample database credentials and Docker socket access. Enterprise features and community features differ. Workflow success is not proof that the business result is correct.

repositories.title: Restore is the test of a backup
repositories.teaching: A backup is a candidate recovery artifact. A restore test is evidence that it can recover the application. Record a known task and timestamp, take a backup, restore into a separate empty database and check contents through the application. Recovery time includes finding the backup, obtaining credentials and validating the result. Data loss is the gap between committed data and what the restored service contains.
repositories.question: A backup job is green. What is still unproven?
repositories.answer: Whether its file is readable, decryption keys are available, schema and application are compatible, expected records exist and recovery finishes within the required time.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Restore five synthetic tasks into a separate database name. Check all titles and completion states, not only the count. Measure elapsed time and retain the source until verification finishes.
repositories.extendedExercise: Seed a disposable database with known records, back it up, deliberately remove only the lab database, restore into a separate clean instance, and run application-level assertions. Record measured recovery time, missing transactions, retention behavior and encryption-key recovery steps.
repositories.expectedEvidence: Prediction, observation, recovery check and explanation saved with lesson evidence.
repositories.doNotCopy: A successful restore job or row count does not prove application consistency. Protect backup credentials and encryption keys separately; keep tests isolated from real data. CI/security assurances in the README were read, not independently reproduced.

repositories.title: An emulator proves only its tested contract
repositories.teaching: An emulator is a local substitute for a cloud API. Configure the application endpoint so the same storage code can address the emulator or AWS. A local object round trip can prove how code handles names and missing data. It cannot establish real account permissions, regional limits, routing or charges. Run a separate check in a disposable cloud scope before trusting those boundaries.
repositories.question: Why can local S3 tests pass while the real upload is denied?
repositories.answer: The emulator may accept fake credentials while AWS evaluates the real principal and policies. Endpoint compatibility and permission correctness are different questions.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Run the same synthetic object round trip locally and later in one temporary AWS bucket. Record missing-object behavior and a deliberately unauthorized identity; compare differences.
repositories.extendedExercise: Write upload/download and missing-object tests against isolated S3 emulation. Inject the endpoint through configuration, use fake local credentials and clean up fixtures. Later run the same contract suite against a temporary AWS bucket, including an explicit access-denied case, and document differences.
repositories.expectedEvidence: Prediction, observation, recovery check and explanation saved with lesson evidence.
repositories.doNotCopy: Passing emulator tests does not validate real IAM, regional behavior, quotas, networking, billing or managed-service availability. Do not claim complete AWS parity from the supported-service list. Avoid mounting the Docker socket unless the chosen test requires it.

repositories.title: Release automation needs a deliberate boundary
repositories.teaching: Release tools demonstrate a useful pattern outside mobile development: validate inputs, prepare an immutable artifact, authenticate with a restricted identity, publish, then verify what users receive. Separate preparation from publication. A machine-readable result helps distinguish an accepted request from a completed release. Temporary signing or access material belongs only in the job that needs it.
repositories.question: Why does a successful build not mean release to users?
repositories.answer: The artifact still requires policy checks, approval, deployment and user-facing verification. Building and publishing are distinct operations with different authority.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Identify the GitLab build, test, promotion and verification jobs. Add a release record with commit, digest and approver; do not publish a mobile app.

repositories.expectedEvidence: Prediction, observation, recovery check and explanation saved with lesson evidence.

repositories.title: A repository clone is not a platform backup
repositories.teaching: Code hosting stores more than commits. Issues, accounts, attachments, packages, settings and credentials can live outside repositories. Recovery must preserve relationships among those stores. Snapshots taken at unrelated moments can leave an issue pointing to a missing attachment. Define the consistency boundary and test actual user operations after restoration.
repositories.question: You recovered every branch. Why might the platform still be unusable?
repositories.answer: Authentication, database records, packages, attachments or configuration can be missing. Repository history is one dependency, not the whole service.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Draw the GitLab service dependencies. Record each recovery owner, backup location, restoration order and a user action that proves recovery. A disposable Gitea restore is an optional extension.
repositories.extendedExercise: Write a source-control service recovery plan covering repositories, database, attachments, configuration and credentials. repositories.expectedEvidence: Prediction, observation, recovery check and explanation saved with lesson evidence.
repositories.doNotCopy: A Git repository mirror is not a complete platform backup. Gitea Actions syntax and runner behavior do not teach GitLab CI directly. Avoid expanding this comparison into a second permanent CI platform.

repositories.title: Correlate slow requests with saturation
repositories.teaching: A host chart is useful when it answers a question about users. Compare request latency with CPU, memory pressure, disk delay and network activity over the same interval. Two rising measurements suggest a hypothesis, not causation. Change one lab condition, repeat the same request and check whether the predicted metric and latency both change.
repositories.question: Memory rises while requests slow. Does that prove insufficient RAM?
repositories.answer: No. Caching may be normal while a database query becomes slower. Check pressure, paging, traces and a controlled repeat before changing capacity.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Collect a quiet baseline, then run a short CPU-bound process in the disposable VM. Observe bounded requests before, during and after load; compare native counters with a dashboard if installed.
repositories.extendedExercise: Create controlled CPU pressure and a slow-disk scenario inside a disposable VM. Correlate latency with CPU, memory, disk and network charts and verify the diagnosis with Linux tools. Write a two-page incident note containing the failed hypothesis as well as the final cause.
repositories.expectedEvidence: Prediction, observation, recovery check and explanation saved with lesson evidence.
repositories.doNotCopy: A dashboard does not supply an SLO or prove causality. Measure collector overhead in the lab rather than accepting marketing performance claims. Review dashboard exposure, host access and telemetry settings; Agent, UI and Cloud have different licensing and service boundaries.

repositories.title: The platform owns the work its button hides
repositories.teaching: A deploy button groups image building, credentials, routing, supervision and persistence. Someone still owns patching, restoration, diagnosis and upgrades. Trace one release and one failure through the platform. A simple managed deployment may reduce operational work; a larger platform is justified by requirements it meets and evidence that the team can operate it.
repositories.question: What must be known before trusting a one-click deployment?
repositories.answer: Who maintains the host, where secrets and data live, what a failed rollout does, how traffic is secured, how restoration works and what it costs.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Compare a VM, managed container service and Dokploy using the course diagram. Give each a host-loss recovery owner and rollback procedure; select by requirements.

repositories.title: Make errors actionable without leaking data
repositories.teaching: An error is easier to diagnose with release, environment, request identifier and failing operation. These connect a user-visible problem to a change. Raw bodies and headers can contain secrets. Redact at collection and inspect the exported event. After fixing the code, add a regression test so the same defect is detected before release.
repositories.question: Why is deleting a secret from a dashboard after export too late?
repositories.answer: It crossed a trust boundary and may persist downstream. Prevent collection or redact before export, then rotate any exposed real secret.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Raise a controlled local exception with a fake token. Inspect serialized telemetry before transmission, prove the token is absent and attach the release identifier.
repositories.extendedExercise: Introduce a controlled exception in staging, attach release/environment metadata, diagnose it from the recorded event, ship a fix and verify the regression test. Demonstrate that a fake password and access token are removed before telemetry leaves the process.
repositories.expectedEvidence: Prediction, observation, recovery check and explanation saved with lesson evidence.
repositories.doNotCopy: Do not treat the whole repository as permissively licensed open source. Error events can carry sensitive application data. The self-hosted documentation site was unavailable during this inspection; no resource sizing or deployment reliability was verified.

repositories.title: Local CI cannot prove the hosted control plane
repositories.teaching: A CI job executes commands; the platform also decides which changes run, which credentials are available and who may release. Local execution helps debug a command but cannot automatically reproduce hosted identity, approvals and concurrency. Translate workflow intent into GitLab, then verify it on the actual runner and protected environment.
repositories.question: A workflow passes locally. What release properties need GitLab evidence?
repositories.answer: Merge-request rules, secret visibility, protected environments, cloud claims, artifact handling, approval policy and deployment serialization.

repositories.doNotCopy: act is not a GitLab CI emulator. A successful local run cannot validate hosted authorization, environment approvals or deployment concurrency. Workflows execute code with the access you grant the runner; inspect them before running.

repositories.title: Reconciliation makes desired state executable
repositories.teaching: GitOps compares desired configuration in Git with cluster resources and reconciles differences. CI tests code and publishes an immutable image; a reviewed configuration change promotes that image. Drift correction, deletion and delivery are separate controls. An unrecorded emergency fix may be overwritten. Recovery should update desired state and separately account for database compatibility.
repositories.question: Why did a manual replica change disappear with self-heal?
repositories.answer: The controller restored Git's desired count. Change approved desired state or deliberately pause reconciliation while recording the emergency operation.
repositories.beginnerExercise: In one namespace, change only replica count and compare self-heal off and on. Revert a bad image reference through Git. Keep pruning disabled until deletion effects are understood.
repositories.extendedExercise: Have GitLab publish an immutable image and propose its digest in an environment repository. Review and merge, observe reconciliation, introduce a harmless replica-count drift, compare self-heal off/on, and revert a bad release through Git. Save timeline evidence and a rollback runbook.
repositories.expectedEvidence: Prediction, observation, recovery check and explanation saved with lesson evidence.
repositories.doNotCopy: Pruning can delete resources and self-heal can overwrite emergency manual edits. Start in an isolated namespace with restrictive access. A Git revert of application manifests does not reverse an incompatible database migration.

repositories.title: Find the process that owns the problem
repositories.teaching: A PID identifies a running process, not the configuration that creates it. A service manager may restart a child after you kill it. Follow the socket to its process, inspect user and parent, then locate the owning service. Fixing the wrong port in that definition addresses the cause; repeatedly killing the child removes only a symptom. Verify helper reports with native tools.
repositories.question: A process returns with a new PID after stopping. What next?
repositories.answer: Inspect parent, service manager, restart policy and unit or container definition. The supervisor may be doing exactly what its configuration requests.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Identify the lesson server with ss and ps. Record PID, user, parent and port, then stop only that lab process. Later compare a restarting systemd service with the helper report.
repositories.extendedExercise: Create a harmless service that keeps restarting and a second service with a port conflict. Identify the owner and launch chain using ps, ss, lsof and systemctl, then compare witr's report. Deliver a runbook that fixes the service definition instead of repeatedly killing a child process.
repositories.expectedEvidence: Prediction, observation, recovery check and explanation saved with lesson evidence.
repositories.doNotCopy: Treat diagnostic output as sensitive because environment and process details may contain secrets. Use inspection operations only during the first exercise; TUI process actions are not read-only. Windows and WSL visibility differ from a Linux server.

repositories.title: Encryption is not authorization or revocation
repositories.teaching: Encrypted configuration can live in Git while approved identities hold decryption authority. File, decryption authority and application secret are three separate things. Removing a recipient from today's file cannot erase yesterday's Git history or invalidate a secret already learned. When access changes, rotate the application credential as well as changing who may decrypt future configuration.
repositories.question: Does removing a recipient revoke their already decrypted database password?
repositories.answer: No. The database accepts it until rotated or disabled. Recipient changes control future decryption, not knowledge already obtained.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Encrypt a dummy value for one local age identity and prove a second cannot decrypt it. Change recipients and rotate the dummy application value; check logs and Git for plaintext.
repositories.extendedExercise: Encrypt fake configuration with age and prove an unauthorized key cannot decrypt it. Later use a tightly scoped cloud identity with KMS, test a denied identity, rotate a recipient, and recover using an approved backup identity. Verify plaintext never appears in CI logs or retained artifacts.
repositories.expectedEvidence: Prediction, observation, recovery check and explanation saved with lesson evidence.
repositories.doNotCopy: Encryption at rest does not protect plaintext after decryption. Removing a recipient cannot erase old Git history or revoke a secret already seen; rotate the actual secret when access is lost. Do not assume Argo CD automatically decrypts SOPS files without a reviewed integration.

repositories.title: Connect three signals to one question
repositories.teaching: Metrics show how frequently a class of requests fails. A trace shows where one request spent time. Logs explain selected events with context. Propagate an identifier to connect the views. More telemetry is not automatically better: unbounded labels, secrets and unlimited retention add cost and risk without necessarily improving diagnosis.
repositories.question: Which evidence links a slow API request to a database call?
repositories.answer: A trace with the database span, correlated log identifiers and latency metrics over the same interval. A host CPU chart alone does not locate that boundary.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Delay one synthetic database operation, find its span and correlate a structured log. Record allowed exported attributes and a justified retention period.
repositories.extendedExercise: Instrument an HTTP request and a database call, propagate a trace identifier, inject a slow query and locate the latency in a trace. Correlate the trace with a structured log and an error-rate metric, then set a justified sampling and retention policy.

repositories.doNotCopy: Telemetry volume, retention and cardinality consume real storage and compute. Do not assume enterprise access controls exist in the community edition. Redact sensitive attributes before export and keep the ingestion endpoint private.

repositories.title: Check the contract, not merely a status code
repositories.teaching: HTTP 200 can carry wrong data. A synthetic check should validate status, selected body fields and a justified latency threshold for a user action. Run monitoring where it can still report when the application fails. Repeated alerts about the same outage add noise; track transitions into failure and recovery.
repositories.question: Why can a green health endpoint coexist with broken task creation?
repositories.answer: The endpoint may only prove the process answers. Creation may still fail on authorization, validation or the database.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Check a task response's status and body. Substitute a wrong but valid 200 response, then stop the app in a separate run. Prove both are detected and recovery clears the failure.
repositories.extendedExercise: Check status code, expected response content and a justified latency threshold. Break DNS, return a misleading HTTP 200 and stop the app in separate drills. Prove each failure is detected, recovery clears it, and notification thresholds avoid repeated noise.
repositories.expectedEvidence: Prediction, observation, recovery check and explanation saved with lesson evidence.
repositories.doNotCopy: Synthetic checks complement rather than replace unit, integration and whole-system tests. A monitor inside the same failed cluster may vanish with the app. Keep credentials out of public check output, and do not make alpha workflow suites a core dependency.

repositories.title: Schema changes must tolerate mixed app versions
repositories.teaching: During a rolling release, old and new application versions coexist. Expand-and-contract first adds compatible schema, then backfills data, switches application use and later removes the old shape. Separate stages permit verification and forward repair. An approval process controls changes but cannot itself prove data is recoverable.
repositories.question: Why can restoring an old image fail after dropping a column?
repositories.answer: Old code still expects the removed schema. Application rollback and database recovery are different operations; destructive changes need staged compatibility.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Add an optional field while retaining the old field. Test both app versions against expanded schema, backfill synthetic records and document the condition required before any removal.
repositories.extendedExercise: Design an expand/contract database change for the capstone. In a disposable PostgreSQL environment, prove that old and new app versions work during the expansion stage, rehearse the data migration and a forward fix, and record who can approve versus execute a change. Inspect Bytebase's workflow; install it only if the required controls are available in the chosen edition.
repositories.expectedEvidence: A migration runbook, compatibility test results and a review/execute permission matrix.
repositories.doNotCopy: A migration rollback button is not proof that data can be recovered. Verify edition entitlements before depending on approval/access features. Avoid importing real database credentials into a learning installation.

repositories.title: A dashboard is an API client
repositories.teaching: A dashboard displays resources using an identity. Its permissions should match the task, like kubectl. repositories.question: Does read-only troubleshooting require cluster-admin?
repositories.answer: No. Grant required read access in the lab namespace. Permission errors require a specific decision, not blanket administrator access.

repositories.doNotCopy: A GUI inherits the power of its credentials. Do not give it cluster-admin merely to remove permission errors; do not publicly expose an administrative dashboard. Choose this or Freelens for the first year, not both.

repositories.title: Failover and backup solve different failures
repositories.teaching: An operator reconciles database resources and may promote another instance after primary failure. Replication can also copy accidental deletion to every replica. A backup plus transaction history recovers an earlier state. Test failover and restoration separately and measure data loss and recovery time. Multiple Pods on one laptop do not prove zone resilience.
repositories.question: Can a healthy standby replace backups?
repositories.answer: No. It may contain the same incorrect change as the primary. Replication and recoverable historical copies address different failures.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Draw primary, standby and backup paths. In the optional operator lab, record timestamped tasks, trigger one primary Pod failure, then independently restore to a new cluster and check contents.
repositories.extendedExercise: In a disposable cluster, follow a release-matched quickstart, write timestamped records, observe primary/standby roles, and simulate a primary Pod failure. Separately back up and restore to a new cluster, verify rows and measure recovery time and data loss. Compare ownership with AWS RDS and Cloud SQL before selecting a database architecture.
repositories.expectedEvidence: Separate failover and restore reports with measured RTO/RPO, checksums or row assertions, and an operator-versus-managed-service decision.
repositories.doNotCopy: Failover and backups solve different problems. A local multi-Pod cluster does not demonstrate availability-zone resilience. Do not copy deprecated backup fields from an old tutorial; match operator, plugin and PostgreSQL documentation to pinned releases.

repositories.title: A finding needs a threat and a verification
repositories.teaching: An audit reports evidence and suggestions. Explain the threat, asset and operational effect before changing configuration. Apply the change reproducibly, rerun the audit and verify the service. Some findings can be accepted with a reason. A higher score alone cannot establish security or compliance.
repositories.question: A hardening change clears a warning but blocks deployment. Complete?
repositories.answer: No. Preserve required operation or revise the deployment design. Record the tradeoff and test both security behavior and the service workflow.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Choose one disposable-VM finding, explain it, apply an Ansible-managed fix and run the application smoke test. Keep before/after evidence and a recovery step.
repositories.extendedExercise: Audit a disposable Linux VM, select three findings whose threat and operational effect you can explain, implement the chosen changes through Ansible, rerun the audit and application smoke tests, and document any intentionally accepted finding.
repositories.expectedEvidence: Before/after findings, three explained fixes, an idempotent Ansible run and regression evidence.
repositories.doNotCopy: The hardening index is not a security guarantee or compliance certificate. Prioritize threat relevance and service functionality over a perfect score. A container or WSL result does not stand in for a complete cloud VM audit.

repositories.title: Separate scheduling authority from build execution
repositories.teaching: A CI controller schedules work; workers execute repository-controlled code. A merge request can alter what a worker runs, so its credentials and host capabilities define a trust boundary. Isolate untrusted checks and keep deployment authority in a narrower approved path. This responsibility split transfers directly to GitLab Runner.
repositories.question: Why avoid arbitrary builds on a CI controller?
repositories.answer: Build scripts gain local access to the service that schedules other work. Isolating execution limits damage from compromised or untrusted jobs.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Draw controller, runner, repository, registry and cloud identity. Mark credentials available to merge-request checks versus the protected deployment job.
repositories.extendedExercise: Map a small Jenkins pipeline's stages, agent, credentials and artifacts onto the equivalent GitLab jobs, runner and variables. Write a short migration note identifying plugin dependencies and the trust boundary between orchestration and executing untrusted code.
repositories.expectedEvidence: A one-page Jenkins-to-GitLab concept map and a runner isolation checklist.
repositories.doNotCopy: Do not spend the main course administering a second CI platform. Installing plugins creates maintenance and security work; a tutorial's plugin list is not an architectural requirement.

repositories.title: Container execution does not erase host authority
repositories.teaching: A container is not a boundary against every host capability. A job with the Docker API may create privileged containers or access host data. Inspect sockets, volumes, credentials and network paths when evaluating runners. Isolation is a property of the full execution configuration, not a YAML label.
repositories.question: Why is mounting the Docker socket a security decision?
repositories.answer: It grants control of the Docker daemon and potentially the host and other workloads. Treat it as execution authority, not an ordinary file.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Annotate mounts and credentials in a runner configuration. Propose disposable build workers and prove untrusted jobs cannot reach deployment credentials.
repositories.extendedExercise: Read the server/agent Compose example and draw which component receives source, runs code and can access credentials. Compare this to GitLab Runner. Explain what mounting the Docker socket grants and propose isolation for untrusted merge requests.
repositories.expectedEvidence: A CI trust-boundary diagram and three isolation controls transferable to GitLab.
repositories.doNotCopy: The example is not a hardened deployment recipe. Docker socket access is a host-control trust decision; copying sample openness or administrator settings is inappropriate for shared runners.

repositories.title: A command interface must preserve failure
repositories.teaching: A task runner names repeatable commands. It should expose the same test logic locally and in CI while preserving nonzero exit codes. Understand the underlying command first. Dependencies and caches need care: skipping a required test can make a release look green without fresh evidence.
repositories.question: What must task test do when one test fails?
repositories.answer: Return failure so the terminal or pipeline stops the release. Printing an error while exiting successfully breaks that contract.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Wrap working unit, integration and system checks with named tasks. Introduce a failing assertion and confirm both local task and GitLab job fail.
repositories.extendedExercise: Create named commands for format, lint, unit, integration, system smoke, build and local teardown. Keep actual logic in understandable scripts or test tools. Have GitLab call the same commands. Prove that a deliberately failing test returns failure to the pipeline and that cleanup stays within the lab.
repositories.expectedEvidence: A documented Taskfile that works from a clean checkout and propagates failing exit codes.
repositories.doNotCopy: Task is an orchestration convenience, not a replacement for shell knowledge or GitLab CI. Untrusted Taskfiles execute commands. A cache or up-to-date shortcut must not silently bypass required validation.

repositories.title: Trace requirements to deployed artifacts
repositories.teaching: A platform should preserve the chain from a reported need through review, tests, artifact and deployment. repositories.question: Does yesterday's passing pipeline prove today's image was tested?

repositories.doNotCopy: The first-year learning value is lifecycle traceability. Operating another full development platform would duplicate GitLab study and add unrelated administration. Root licensing does not establish entitlements for every external plugin or hosted feature.

repositories.title: Limit release exposure while measuring behavior
repositories.teaching: A gateway can send some requests to a new version. Risk falls only when versions are compatible and signals reveal regressions. Define thresholds and stop conditions before traffic. Keep management access private and test authentication, throttling and upstream failure separately.
repositories.question: Is ten-percent canary traffic automatically safe?
repositories.answer: No. It can still corrupt shared data, and silent errors need meaningful checks. Compatibility and tested traffic rollback are required.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Use two local versions and a small request sample. Record version, correctness and latency; restore all traffic to the known version after an injected defect.
repositories.extendedExercise: Put two capstone versions behind a disposable gateway, route a small percentage of requests to the new version, enforce authentication and a rate limit, then test unauthorized, throttled, healthy and unavailable-upstream responses. Record latency before and after the gateway and rehearse rollback.
repositories.expectedEvidence: Versioned route policy, automated HTTP assertions, a small latency comparison and rollback evidence.
repositories.doNotCopy: A gateway adds another component to operate. Keep the management API private. Do not copy a remote shell quickstart into a production host; inspect and pin artifacts. Choose one gateway implementation for the exercise.

repositories.question: Why separate template editing from execution?

repositories.title: Edge filtering complements application correctness
repositories.teaching: A WAF recognizes selected request patterns. Ownership of a user's task is business context enforced by the application. Keep authorization tests, then add edge controls and test legitimate and suspicious requests. Tune narrow false positives instead of disabling all rules.
repositories.question: Can a WAF replace a cross-user access test?
repositories.answer: No. The application must enforce ownership regardless of filtering at the edge.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Retain two-user access tests. Run a local request corpus with valid punctuation and controlled suspicious strings, tune one false positive and rerun allowed and denied cases.
repositories.extendedExercise: Protect only your disposable capstone service. Create a small regression suite with legitimate requests and controlled malicious-looking inputs, observe false positives, make one narrow rule exception, and prove legitimate traffic works without disabling the entire rule set.
repositories.expectedEvidence: A request/expected-result matrix, a justified narrow exception, relevant logs and a configuration rollback.
repositories.doNotCopy: A WAF does not repair broken authorization, vulnerable code or exposed credentials. Test only owned lab endpoints, retain application tests, and evaluate edition/licensing requirements before adoption. The linked security-tuning page could not be retrieved in this audit.

repositories.title: Incidents are a coordination loop

repositories.doNotCopy: A full self-hosted deployment should not be mandatory on an unknown laptop or cloud budget. Demonstrated features and automated-fix marketing are not evidence of diagnosis accuracy. Check current sizing and paid/external notification costs before a later trial.

repositories.answer: Current task prerequisites and demonstrated learner gaps. Teach a dependency before the tool that relies on it.
repositories.beginnerExercise: During quarterly review, choose one weak capability, define an acceptance check and complete it before adding optional tooling.
repositories.extendedExercise: Compare completed capability evidence with its major categories during quarterly review.
repositories.expectedEvidence: A prioritized missing-capability list and one justification for a tool choice.
repositories.doNotCopy: Its resource list is not a tested lab sequence. It includes paid and free learning resources; purchasing anything is optional. Keep software engineering practices and security in the main path rather than postponing them.

repositories.title: An extension creates an operating obligation
repositories.teaching: Add-ons introduce APIs, privileges, configuration and upgrade dependencies. State the missing capability, maintainer, failure behavior and removal plan before installing. Shortlist using primary docs and supported versions. A local function test is separate from resilience and upgrade evidence.
repositories.question: What proves a network policy solution works?
repositories.answer: Supported cluster integration and a denied-traffic test. Creating a policy object without an enforcing network plugin proves nothing about blocked packets.
repositories.beginnerExercise: For one add-on, record purpose, permissions, compatibility, failure signal, rollback and removal. Reject it if existing components already satisfy the requirement.
repositories.extendedExercise: Start with one question, shortlist at most two options, and validate against their official documentation.
repositories.expectedEvidence: A short architecture decision describing requirements, costs, maintenance and the rejected option.
repositories.doNotCopy: Historical articles and platform names remain in the list. Directory inclusion does not establish maintenance, compatibility or security. Do not add service mesh, multiple ingress products and extra operators without a concrete need.

repositories.title: Reliability is a measured promise
repositories.teaching: Define a useful user action and measure success within a meaningful latency threshold. An SLO states the target over a window; an error budget describes allowed bad events. This makes release tradeoffs explicit. Alert on actionable conditions, write symptom runbooks and examine contributing conditions after incidents.
repositories.question: Why is average response time insufficient?
repositories.answer: It hides a minority of slow requests. A threshold-based proportion or relevant percentile exposes the experience the objective protects.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Define a Taskboard SLI from success counts and latency. Calculate good/total from a sample, inject a brief failure and connect the alert to a runbook.
repositories.extendedExercise: Select one primary SRE chapter or operator case study, then apply it through an incident or measurement exercise.
repositories.expectedEvidence: SLO specification, actionable alert, runbook, incident timeline, postmortem and verified follow-up improvement.
repositories.doNotCopy: Reading is paired with the learner's own evidence. Some links are historical; use current primary destinations where available. Simulated on-call experience must be described as simulation.

repositories.title: Separate platform faults from application faults
repositories.teaching: A known service with health endpoints and fault controls helps isolate platform behavior. Prove routing and rollout there, then repeat with Taskboard. Readiness governs normal Service traffic; liveness restarts failed processes; startup protects initialization. A working reference app does not prove your business rules, database or migration.
repositories.question: What does a working reference workload establish?
repositories.answer: It exercises some shared platform paths, strengthening app-specific configuration and dependency hypotheses. It narrows diagnosis without proving the entire platform.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Observe readiness failure and a bad-image rollout on the reference service, record events and endpoints, recover, then repeat on Taskboard.
repositories.extendedExercise: Use it to isolate platform problems, then transfer its tested practices to the learner's business application.
repositories.expectedEvidence: GitLab translation of relevant test stages; readiness and rollout experiments; a fault-injection incident with metrics and recovery evidence.
repositories.doNotCopy: The app intentionally exposes /env, /configs, /panic and fault controls; keep it private with dummy values. Workflow labels use both integration and end-to-end terms; classify your tests by the actual boundary they exercise. Its ready-made application does not replace business-rule, database migration or recovery testing of the main project. Inspect the tested source revision rather than copying an unpinned latest chart.

repositories.title: Make a reviewable tool decision
repositories.teaching: A decision record states problem, constraints, alternatives, chosen approach and reconsideration evidence. Include permissions, cost, maintenance and recovery. Keep research bounded so it becomes a tested service improvement instead of a bookmark collection.
repositories.question: What makes a decision better than a feature list?
repositories.answer: It connects the choice to service needs and records tradeoffs, ownership and reversal conditions for another engineer to assess.
repositories.beginnerExercise: Compare two candidates for one real course problem, perform an acceptance test with the choice and specify a reassessment trigger.
repositories.extendedExercise: Use a category to find two candidates for a real requirement and continue in primary project documentation.
repositories.expectedEvidence: A decision record with the operational cost of adopting the chosen tool.
repositories.doNotCopy: Tags and list membership do not verify license suitability, maintenance or secure defaults. Limit fault experiments to the owned lab and document scope and stop conditions. The selected stack remains stable unless evidence warrants a change.
